title: Atomic-scale control of spin transport in exchange-coupled molecules
authors: A. Fétida, R. Robles, F. Scheurer, M. Romeo, J. Kröger, N. Lorente, L. Limot
abstract: Spin transport between coupled spins is governed by tunneling and exchange interactions, yet their microscopic relation in real space has remained experimentally elusive. To address this, we functionalize the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope with a single molecule and use it as a movable spin sensor positioned above a second molecule on a ferromagnetic surface, forming an exchange-coupled molecular junction. From the same spectroscopic dataset, we independently extract the junction conductance, exchange coupling, and spin polarization with atomic-scale resolution. Conductance and exchange display nearly identical spatial dependences, consistent with a minimal Hubbard description in which both are governed by the same hopping matrix between the molecular frontier orbitals. In contrast, the spin polarization depends on the orbital composition and the relative weight of the resulting transport channels. These results establish a real-space connection between tunneling, exchange, and spin transport in magnetically coupled molecules.
summary: This work experimentally and theoretically links charge transport, magnetic exchange, and spin polarization in molecular junctions using STM. By simultaneously mapping these three quantities, the authors demonstrate that while conductance and exchange coupling follow similar spatial rules governed by hopping, the spin polarization is highly sensitive to the specific orbital structure of the junction. This establishes a fundamental, real-space understanding of spin transport in molecular magnets.
main_problem: To establish a real-space connection between tunneling, exchange, and spin transport in magnetically coupled molecules.
main_result: The study shows that conductance and exchange coupling share similar spatial dependencies, suggesting both are governed by the same hopping matrix, while spin polarization depends on the specific orbital composition.
method: The researchers used STM spectroscopy to simultaneously extract junction conductance, exchange coupling, and spin polarization from a single dataset, complemented by DFT calculations.
model_or_system: The system involves an exchange-coupled molecular junction formed between a single molecule functionalized on an STM tip and a second molecule adsorbed on a ferromagnetic surface (e.g., Co islands). The physics is modeled using a minimal Hubbard description for the molecular interaction.
key_observables: Junction conductance, exchange coupling strength ($E_{ex}$), and spin polarization ($P$) mapped spatially across the junction.
important_parameters: The hopping matrix elements between molecular frontier orbitals, which dictate the coupling strength and transport channels.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a minimal Hubbard description governs the coupling, and the conductance calculation employs Bardeen’s tunneling formalism.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate STM images, simulated conductance maps, spin-excitation spectra showing characteristic splittings, and spatial maps detailing the variation of exchange energy and spin polarization across the junction.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by characterizing the physical setup (molecular junction), measuring multiple correlated quantities (G, $E_{ex}$, P) from one dataset, relating their spatial dependencies to a common underlying hopping mechanism, and finally detailing how orbital composition dictates the measured spin polarization.
why_interesting: The direct, real-space measurement and theoretical linkage between charge transport (conductance) and magnetic coupling (exchange/spin polarization) in molecular junctions provides a powerful experimental realization of correlated electron physics in nanoscale systems.
